title: Is Haunted Hotel A Kids' Show? Think Gravity Falls for Adults
excerpt: Haunted Hotel shares a lot of the same comedic spirit and thematic weight as Gravity Falls, but it’s a far cry from the kid-friendly horror show.
content:
Haunted Hotel (2025) is one of Netflix’s most pleasant recent surprises, a goofy horror-tinted comedy that blends the sitcom-y elements of The Simpsons (1989) with the surreal and flexible terror of The Twilight Zone (1959). The show never loses sight of its comedy tone, heartfelt core, and frightening tropes, which is likely why it did so well on the streaming platform. It also helps that this is a formula that’s been refined over the years.

The episodic supernatural show has been around for a while, with plenty of properties like Buffy the Vampire Slayer (1997) finding ways to infuse grounded emotional drama into the mix. One of the best examples of that style of show is the cult classic Disney animated series, Gravity Falls (2012), which took that tone and played it so well that kids and adults could fall in love with it. Although Haunted Hotel is a much more adult show, it’s playing with a lot of the same creative touchstones as Gravity Falls. Still, it’s best reserved for teens (or perhaps older children with adult supervision).

Haunted Hotel might have a similar underlying tone and animation style to Gravity Falls, but the Netflix comedy is definitely not for kids. Like Gravity Falls, the show focuses on a family who find themselves contending with both the mundane and the mysterious while in a remote part of the country. Whereas Gravity Falls focused on twins Dipper and Mabel with their Grunkle Stan and his employees Soos and Wendy, Haunted Hotel expands the focus to Ben and Esther along with their mother Katherine, uncle Nathan, and adopted housemate Abaddon. 

The general sense of horrifying whimsy is at play here, although Haunted Hotel’s more mature sense of humor means the scares get to be a lot more grisly and unsettling. However, both shows have an eye for overarching plots and themes about family coming first even in an absurd world, all with a supernatural bent. Although Haunted Hotel shares a lot of DNA with Gravity Falls, it’s not necessarily something that kids should jump into right after finishing the modern Disney classic. However, older audiences with a love for Dipper and Mabel’s adventures will find plenty to love about the show.

'Haunted Hotel's Worldbuilding Makes for Limitless Comedy

Haunted Hotel has one of the chief strengths that always helped Gravity Falls, and that’s the open sandbox that comes with the world. There’s been no firm explanation for the full scope of Haunted Hotel’s universe, allowing for a slew of parodies that can explore the horror genre as a whole. The first season had plenty of riffs on things like Jason Voorhees and Ghost Hunters (2004), coupled with some unique reimaginings of common supernatural storytelling and folklore. 

It’s all filtered through a sitcom-style formula, where each episode includes silly cameos from any number of bizarre ghosts that inhabit the building. It’s similar to the way Gravity Falls naturally built out its own mythology, with lots of strange little touches that helped it stand out. Haunted Hotel gets to fully embrace the full scope of horror stories, giving it room to do a potentially limitless number of parodies of the genre, all within its own imagining of the world. That narrative freedom and sense of comedy intermixed with horror is another way Netflix’s Haunted Hotel remixes the Gravity Falls formula for Adult Swim-style comedy.

What to Know About 'Haunted Hotel' Season 2 (And Beyond)

Haunted Hotel is poised to release its second season right in the middle of the Halloween season. The trailer for Haunted Hotel Season 2 teases parodies of Hellraiser (1987) and The Ring (2002), as well as suggesting a new cast member will be the teenage supernatural expert who seems like an equivalent to Wendy from Gravity Falls. Netflix hasn’t yet confirmed if the show will continue beyond Season 2, although the massive creative potential of the series makes it ideal for the streaming platform to continue to expand upon. 

This expansion of the cast and tweak on the formula speaks to the way that shows like Haunted Hotel can evolve and shift as time goes on. There are also the emotional teases that were introduced in the first season (like the fact that Nathan is a ghost because he took his own life and Abaddon’s struggles with embracing his newfound family). There’s lots of room for the show to play with, especially if it continues to do as well for Netflix as the first season did. Ideal for people who grew up with (or just fell in love with) Gravity Falls but want something a bit more mature, Haunted Hotel might be the funniest way to frighten yourself this Halloween season.
